segments.en: Listen closely and you might hear it: a fiddle, a tin whistle and the soft beat of a bodhrán drum, drifting out of a pub on a damp evening. That is a session, and anyone is welcome to pull up a stool and listen.
You're in Ireland, an island on the western edge of Europe where the Atlantic sets the mood. Sunshine and showers can take turns all afternoon, which is exactly why the fields are so famously green.

Irish people love a good conversation. Ask for directions and you may get a story, a joke and a weather report before you learn where to turn. The word for that lively fun is craic, as in, what's the craic?

Two languages share this island. English is heard everywhere, but Irish, an ancient Celtic language, lives on in schools, on road signs and in Gaeltacht communities along the west coast. A friendly hello is Dia duit.

Dublin, the capital, sits where the River Liffey meets the sea. It is a city of writers, home to James Joyce and Oscar Wilde, and it keeps the Book of Kells, a glowing painted manuscript made by monks more than a thousand years ago.
Head west and the land turns wild. The Cliffs of Moher drop straight into the ocean, and in Connemara, grey stone walls wander over the hills between lakes, bogs and grazing sheep.

Older than any castle is Newgrange, a great passage tomb built more than five thousand years ago. Around the shortest day of winter, the rising sun slips down its stone passage and lights the chamber inside.

Sport here is played with real passion. Hurling is a lightning-fast game with wooden sticks and a small leather ball, and Gaelic football is just as loved. The players are amateurs, proudly representing their parish and county.
Food is hearty and comforting. Try a bowl of Irish stew, brown soda bread still warm from the oven, or a full Irish breakfast. By the coast, fresh oysters and smoked salmon are local treasures.
On the seventeenth of March, Saint Patrick's Day fills streets around the world with green. At home it is a family holiday too, with parades, music and a sprig of shamrock pinned to a coat.
Before you go, share a cup of tea, the real national drink, and say slán, which means goodbye. Then look east: just across the Irish Sea, the United Kingdom is waiting.
